desc:
A grid is an integer matrix. The values mean: 1 the start cell, 2 the end cell, 3 a required cell, 0 an ordinary free cell, and -1 a blocked cell that can never be entered. There is exactly one start and exactly one end cell, and there may be any number of required cells.

A route begins on the start cell and moves one step at a time up, down, left or right. It may not enter a blocked cell and may not visit any cell twice. The route finishes the first time it reaches the end cell. Return the number of routes that visit every required cell before finishing. Ordinary free cells may be visited or skipped, and two routes are different when they visit their cells in a different order.

For example, in [[1,3,2],[0,0,0]] the answer is 3: the direct walk along the top row, and two walks that dip into the bottom row and climb back to the top row through the required cell; in [[1,0,2]] there is one route and no cell is required, so it counts.
constraints: Exactly one cell is 1 and exactly one cell is 2
hints: Count the required cells first. A finished route is only valid if none is left over when it reaches the end.
Run a DFS from the start with a visited grid and a counter left of required cells still unvisited. Entering a required cell decreases the counter.

At the end cell return 1 if left == 0 and 0 otherwise, and never walk on from the end cell. Elsewhere mark the cell, add up the results for all open unvisited neighbours, and unmark the cell on the way back.
editorial: Compared with counting all routes between two cells, the only new ingredient is the counter of required cells that have not been seen yet. It is passed down the recursion (so it needs no undo), and it is checked only at the end cell: a route that arrives there with required cells left is simply not counted. The route cannot continue past the end cell, because the end cell may not be visited twice.

The search enumerates the routes, so its cost grows with the number of routes between the two cells in a grid of at most 25 cells (at most about 9,000 on a 25-cell board). Pruning is possible, for example abandoning a branch as soon as a required cell can no longer be reached, but it is not required.
